intro: Practice in your own AWS account with free credits. Each lab gives console steps, what you should see, and a clean-up list. Console labels change over time, so if a button’s name differs slightly, pick the closest match. Use one Region for all labs.

labs.title: Secure your account and set cost guardrails
labs.goal: Protect the root user with MFA, create a budget alert, and set up a separate admin sign-in before any other lab.
labs.why: Root user protection, MFA, least privilege, and AWS Budgets are tested in Domains 2 and 4, and these steps keep your practice account safe.
prerequisites: An AWS account that you own. New accounts get credits; check your plan in step 6.
An authenticator app on your phone or a security key.
steps: Sign in as the root user (the email address that created the account).
Open the account menu (top right) → Security credentials → Assign MFA device. Choose a passkey or security key, or an authenticator app, and finish the setup.
On the same page, check “Access keys”. The root user should have none; delete any that exist.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Budgets → Create budget → Use a template → Zero spend budget. Enter your email address and create it.
Create a second budget with the “Monthly cost budget” template, set an amount such as $5, and keep the email alerts.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Credits (and the Free Tier page) to see your credits, when they expire, and whether you are on the free plan or a paid plan.
Open Billing preferences and turn on AWS Free Tier usage alerts if the option is available for your account.

Open IAM Identity Center → Enable (this also turns on AWS Organizations, which is free). Create a user for yourself, create a permission set from the AdministratorAccess policy, and assign both to your account.
Note the AWS access portal URL, sign out, and sign in through the portal as your new user. Register MFA when asked.
Pick one Region (for example the one closest to you) and use it for every lab.
check: Security credentials shows an MFA device for the root user and no root access keys.
Budgets lists the zero-spend budget and the monthly budget.
You can sign in through the access portal and open the console as your Identity Center user.
tips: From now on, use your Identity Center user for labs and keep the root user for the few tasks that need it.
New accounts can earn extra credits for activities such as creating a budget; check the Explore AWS widget on Console Home.

labs.title: IAM least privilege in practice
labs.goal: Create a group with read-only S3 access, test what a member can and can’t do, and review credentials.
labs.why: Users, groups, policies, least privilege, the policy simulator, and the credential report are all Domain 2 topics.
steps: Open IAM → User groups → Create group named lab-readonly and attach the AWS managed policy AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.
Open IAM → Users → Create user named lab-tester, allow console access with an autogenerated password, and add it to lab-readonly.
Copy the account sign-in URL from the IAM dashboard and sign in as lab-tester in a private browser window.
As lab-tester, open S3 and list buckets (allowed). Then try to create a bucket (denied).
Back as your admin user, open the IAM policy simulator, select lab-tester, and simulate s3:ListAllMyBuckets and s3:CreateBucket.
Open IAM → Credential report → Download and look at the MFA and access key columns for each user.
check: Listing buckets works but creating one fails with an access denied message.
The policy simulator shows “allowed” for the list action and “denied” for the create action.
The credential report shows lab-tester without MFA.
cleanup: Delete the user lab-tester.
Delete the group lab-readonly.
tips: Permissions come from policies attached to groups; this is easier to manage than per-user policies.

labs.title: Launch a web server on Amazon EC2
labs.goal: Launch an instance with a web page, connect to it, compare stop and terminate, and back up its volume.
labs.why: EC2 instances, AMIs, security groups, instance states, EBS, and snapshots appear across Domains 2, 3, and 4.
labs.costNote: About $0.02 an hour for a free-tier-eligible instance and its public IPv4 address, covered by credits. Terminate it when done.
steps: Open EC2 → Launch instance. Name it lab-web, choose Amazon Linux 2023, and pick an instance type marked “Free tier eligible”.
Under Key pair choose “Proceed without a key pair”. Under Network settings, create a security group lab-web-sg that allows HTTP from anywhere and SSH from My IP.

Paste this into Advanced details → User data: #!/bin/bash dnf install -y httpd echo "

Hello from $(hostname -f)

" > /var/www/html/index.html systemctl enable --now httpd
Launch the instance and wait until its state is Running and both status checks pass.
Copy the instance’s public IPv4 address and open http://<address> in your browser.
Select the instance → Connect → EC2 Instance Connect → Connect, then run: curl localhost
Stop the instance, then start it again. Compare the public IP address before and after.
Open the Storage tab, select the root volume, and choose Actions → Create snapshot named lab-web-snap.
Open the instance’s Monitoring tab to see CPU and network metrics from CloudWatch.
check: The browser shows “Hello from …” with the instance’s host name.
The public IP address changes after a stop and start, but the files on the EBS volume remain.
The snapshot appears under Elastic Block Store → Snapshots.
cleanup: Terminate lab-web (this deletes its root volume by default).
Delete the snapshot lab-web-snap.
Delete the security group lab-web-sg after the instance is terminated.
tips: A stopped instance doesn’t pay for compute, but EBS storage is still charged.
New accounts can earn credits for launching an EC2 instance.

labs.title: Store and protect data in Amazon S3
labs.goal: Create a bucket, use versioning to recover a deleted file, add a lifecycle rule, and host a static web page.
labs.why: S3 storage classes, lifecycle policies, Block Public Access, encryption, and versioning are Domain 2 and 3 topics.
labs.costNote: Fractions of a cent for a few small files. Delete the buckets when done.
steps: Open S3 → Create bucket named lab-s3-<your initials and a number>. Keep Block Public Access on and default encryption (SSE-S3) on.
Open the bucket → Properties → Bucket Versioning → Enable.
Upload a small text file, edit it on your computer, and upload it again with the same name.
Turn on “Show versions” to see both versions. Delete the object, see the delete marker, then delete the marker to restore the file.
Open Management → Create lifecycle rule lab-archive for the whole bucket: move current versions to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 30 days and expire noncurrent versions after 60 days.
Create a second bucket lab-site-<number>. Upload an index.html file containing a short message.
In lab-site → Properties → Static website hosting → Enable, with index.html as the index document. Open the website endpoint: it returns 403 Forbidden.
Reload the website endpoint.
check: Deleting the object in a versioned bucket only adds a delete marker, and the file comes back when you delete the marker.
The lifecycle rule shows its transition and expiration actions.
The website returns 403 while Block Public Access is on, and shows your page after the policy is added.
cleanup: Empty both buckets (including all versions), then delete them.
Confirm that account-level Block Public Access is still on (S3 → Block Public Access settings for this account).
tips: Block Public Access overrides bucket policies, which is why the site stayed private until you turned it off.

labs.title: Build a serverless web endpoint with AWS Lambda
labs.goal: Create a Lambda function, give it a public URL, and find its logs in CloudWatch.
labs.why: Serverless compute, pay-per-request pricing, and CloudWatch Logs are Domain 3 topics.
steps: Open Lambda → Create function → Author from scratch. Name it lab-hello and choose the latest Python runtime.
Choose Test, create a test event with the default template, and run it.
Open Configuration → Function URL → Create function URL, choose auth type NONE, and save. Open the URL.
Open Monitor → View CloudWatch logs and look at the log stream for your invocations.
check: The test shows a 200 status code and the HTML body.
The function URL shows “Hello from Lambda” in the browser.
CloudWatch Logs has a log group /aws/lambda/lab-hello with START and END lines for each run.
cleanup: Delete the function URL and then the function lab-hello.
Delete the log group /aws/lambda/lab-hello in CloudWatch.
tips: There is no server to patch: AWS runs and scales the function, and you pay only per request and run time.
New accounts can earn credits for creating a web app with Lambda.

labs.title: Compare DynamoDB and Amazon RDS
labs.goal: Create a NoSQL table and a small relational database, and look at backup and availability settings.
labs.why: Choosing between NoSQL and relational databases, Multi-AZ, and backups are Domain 3 topics.
labs.costNote: DynamoDB stays within always-free limits. A free-tier-template RDS instance costs about $0.02 an hour if not covered; delete it the same day.
steps: Open DynamoDB → Create table lab-orders with partition key customerId (String) and sort key orderId (String). Use on-demand capacity.
Open Explore items and create three items for two different customers, adding an attribute such as total.
Run a Query for one customerId and notice that it returns only that customer’s orders.
Open RDS → Create database. Choose MySQL or PostgreSQL and the Free tier template. Name it lab-db, let AWS generate a password, and keep Public access set to No.
While it is being created (about 10 minutes), read the Availability and durability section: note that Multi-AZ isn’t available in this template.
Open lab-db → Maintenance & backups and note the automated backup retention period and the maintenance window.
check: DynamoDB returns items in milliseconds without any server or capacity settings.
RDS shows the engine, instance class, storage, a single AZ, and automated backups.
cleanup: Delete lab-db: clear “Create final snapshot” and “Retain automated backups”, and confirm.
Delete the DynamoDB table lab-orders.
tips: For production, Multi-AZ adds a standby in another AZ for high availability; read replicas add read capacity.
New accounts can earn credits for creating an RDS database.

labs.title: Build a VPC and test security groups vs network ACLs
labs.goal: Create a VPC with public and private subnets, then see how security groups and network ACLs filter traffic.
labs.why: VPC components, internet gateways, and stateful vs stateless filtering are frequent Domain 2 and 3 questions.
labs.costNote: The VPC is free. The test instance costs about $0.02 an hour. Don’t add a NAT gateway (it costs about $0.045 an hour).
steps: Open VPC → Create VPC → VPC and more. Name it lab, choose 2 Availability Zones, 2 public and 2 private subnets, NAT gateways: None, and VPC endpoints: None.
Open the resource map: find the internet gateway and the route table whose 0.0.0.0/0 route points to it (public subnets).

Launch an EC2 instance named lab-vpc-web in one of the lab public subnets with auto-assign public IP enabled, a new security group allowing HTTP from anywhere, and this user data: #!/bin/bash dnf install -y httpd echo "

VPC lab

" > /var/www/html/index.html systemctl enable --now httpd
Open http://<public IP> to confirm the page loads.
Open the network ACL associated with that subnet and add inbound rule number 90: DENY, HTTP (80), source 0.0.0.0/0. Reload the page.
Delete the deny rule and reload: the page works again.
Remove the HTTP inbound rule from the instance’s security group and reload. Then add it back.
check: The network ACL deny rule blocks the page even though the security group allows HTTP.
Without an HTTP inbound rule, the security group blocks the page; you never needed an outbound rule for responses (stateful).
cleanup: Terminate lab-vpc-web and wait until it is terminated.
Delete the VPC named lab (this removes its subnets, route tables, internet gateway, network ACLs, and security groups).
tips: Network ACLs are stateless and evaluate rules in number order; the lowest matching rule wins.

labs.title: High availability with a load balancer and Auto Scaling
labs.goal: Run a web app on an Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind a load balancer, and watch it heal itself.
labs.why: Elasticity, high availability across AZs, load balancing, and Auto Scaling are core Domain 1 and 3 ideas.
labs.costNote: About $0.05–0.10 an hour for two instances and the load balancer. Finish in one sitting and delete everything.
steps: Open EC2 → Launch templates → Create launch template lab-web-lt: Amazon Linux 2023, a free-tier-eligible instance type, a security group allowing HTTP from anywhere, and the user data from the EC2 lab.
Open EC2 → Auto Scaling groups → Create Auto Scaling group lab-asg using lab-web-lt. Select the default VPC and subnets in at least two Availability Zones.
Choose “Attach to a new load balancer”: Application Load Balancer, internet-facing, with a new target group. Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks.
Set desired capacity 2, minimum 2, maximum 4, and add a target tracking policy for 50% average CPU. Create the group.
When the instances are healthy, open the load balancer’s DNS name and refresh several times.
In EC2 → Instances, terminate one of the lab-asg instances. Watch the group’s Activity tab.
Edit the group and set desired capacity to 3. Watch a new instance start.
check: Refreshing the load balancer page shows different host names, so traffic is spread across instances.
After you terminate an instance, Auto Scaling launches a replacement automatically.
Raising the desired capacity adds an instance (scaling out).
cleanup: Delete the Auto Scaling group lab-asg (this terminates its instances).
Delete the load balancer and then the target group.
Delete the launch template lab-web-lt and its security group.
tips: High availability = multiple AZs + a load balancer + Auto Scaling.

labs.title: Infrastructure as code with AWS CloudFormation
labs.goal: Create, update, check for drift, and delete a stack from a template.
labs.why: Infrastructure as code and repeatable deployments are Domain 3 topics (task 3.1).
steps:
Save this template on your computer as lab-stack.yaml:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Description: CLF lab stack
Resources:
  LabBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
  LabTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Properties:
      TopicName: lab-cfn-topic
Outputs:
  BucketName:
    Value: !Ref LabBucket
Open CloudFormation → Create stack → With new resources → Upload a template file, choose lab-stack.yaml, and name the stack lab-stack.
Watch the Events tab until the status is CREATE_COMPLETE, then open the Resources and Outputs tabs.
In S3, open the new bucket and suspend versioning manually. Back in CloudFormation, choose Stack actions → Detect drift and view the drift results.

Edit the template to add a tag under the bucket’s Properties, then choose Update stack → Replace existing template and review the change set before you confirm:
      Tags:
        - Key: project
          Value: clf-lab
check: The stack creates a bucket and an SNS topic, and the bucket name appears in Outputs.
Drift detection reports the bucket as MODIFIED after your manual change.
The change set shows that the bucket will be modified, not replaced.
cleanup: Delete the stack lab-stack. CloudFormation deletes the topic and the (empty) bucket.
tips: Deleting a stack deletes everything it created, which makes clean-up easy.

labs.title: Monitor and audit with CloudTrail, CloudWatch, and Config
labs.goal: Find who did what with CloudTrail, get an email alarm from CloudWatch, and check compliance with Config.
labs.why: Domain 2 asks which service audits API activity, monitors metrics, and records configuration compliance.
labs.costNote: CloudTrail event history and up to 10 CloudWatch alarms are free. AWS Config costs fractions of a cent per recorded change; stop recording when done.
steps: Open CloudTrail → Event history. Filter by Event name (for example TerminateInstances or DeleteBucket from earlier labs) and open an event to see who did it, when, and from which IP address.
Open SNS → Topics → Create topic (Standard) named lab-alerts. Create a subscription with protocol Email and your address, then confirm it from your inbox.
Open Billing preferences and turn on CloudWatch billing alerts. Switch to the US East (N. Virginia) Region, where billing metrics are stored.
Open CloudWatch → Alarms → Create alarm → Billing → Total Estimated Charge. Set the threshold to greater than $1 and notify lab-alerts.
Switch back to your lab Region. Open AWS Config → Get started (1-click setup) to start recording resources.
Add the managed rule s3-bucket-versioning-enabled and wait for its evaluation.
check: CloudTrail shows the user, time, source IP, and request details of past actions.
The alarm exists and the email subscription is confirmed.
Config lists resources and marks buckets without versioning as noncompliant.
cleanup: In Config, delete the rule and stop recording (Settings → stop the recorder).
Keep the billing alarm if you want ongoing protection; otherwise delete it and the lab-alerts topic.
tips: CloudTrail = who did what. Config = what the configuration was and whether it complies. CloudWatch = how things perform.

labs.title: Decouple with SNS, SQS, and EventBridge
labs.goal: Fan out one message to two queues and send scheduled events, without writing code.
labs.why: Choosing between SQS, SNS, and EventBridge is a common Domain 3 question (task 3.8).
steps: Open SQS → Create queue (Standard) named lab-billing, then another named lab-shipping.
Open SNS → Create topic (Standard) named lab-orders.
Open each queue → Subscribe to Amazon SNS topic → choose lab-orders. (The console adds the queue permissions for you.)
Open the topic lab-orders → Publish message, with a body such as {"order": 42}.
Open each queue → Send and receive messages → Poll for messages, and open the message.

Open EventBridge → Schedules → Create schedule lab-every-5-min with a rate of 5 minutes. Choose the SNS Publish target lab-orders with a short JSON payload, and let the console create the execution role.
check: One published message appears in both queues (fan-out).
Every five minutes, new messages from the schedule arrive in both queues.
cleanup: Delete the schedule lab-every-5-min and its execution role.
Delete the topic lab-orders and its subscriptions.
Delete the queues lab-billing and lab-shipping.
tips: SNS pushes to many subscribers; SQS holds messages until a consumer pulls them.

labs.title: Tour the security services
labs.goal: See sample threat findings, a security posture score, Trusted Advisor checks, and an AWS compliance report.
labs.why: Domain 2 tests which security service does what, and where to find AWS compliance documents.
steps: Open GuardDuty → Get started → Enable GuardDuty (30-day free trial). Open Settings → Generate sample findings.
Open Findings and read two sample findings: their severity, the affected resource, and the recommended remediation.
Open Security Hub and enable it with the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard (free trial). Later, view the security score and findings, including the imported GuardDuty findings.
Open Amazon Inspector → Activate (free trial) and look at the coverage page: it lists the EC2 instances, container images, and Lambda functions it can scan.
Open Trusted Advisor → Recommendations and review the Security category (for example MFA on the root account).
Open AWS Artifact → Reports, search for “SOC 2”, and view the report details.
check: GuardDuty shows sample findings such as unusual API calls or cryptocurrency mining.
Security Hub shows a security score and failed controls.
Trusted Advisor shows security checks with their status.
cleanup: Disable Amazon Inspector (deactivate all scan types).
Disable Security Hub.
Suspend or disable GuardDuty before the 30-day trial ends.
tips: Detect threats → GuardDuty; vulnerabilities → Inspector; one dashboard → Security Hub; compliance reports → Artifact.

labs.title: Estimate, track, and allocate costs
labs.goal: Estimate a project with the Pricing Calculator, explore Cost Explorer, and activate a cost allocation tag.
labs.why: Domain 4 asks which tool estimates, alerts on, analyzes, and allocates costs.
steps: Open the AWS Pricing Calculator and create an estimate: two small EC2 instances running all month, one small RDS database, and 50 GB of S3 Standard.
In the EC2 part of the estimate, compare On-Demand pricing with a 1-year Compute Savings Plan.
Open Billing and Cost Management → Cost Explorer. Group costs by Service, switch to daily granularity, and view the forecast. (The first time, data can take up to 24 hours to appear.)
Open Bills to see charges by service and any credits applied.
Tag a lab resource (for example an S3 bucket) with CostCenter = lab. Then open Cost allocation tags and activate CostCenter.
Open Compute Optimizer and opt in. It needs some running time before it shows recommendations.
check: The estimate shows a monthly total and a lower price with the Savings Plan.
Cost Explorer shows your spend by service with a forecast.
The CostCenter tag shows as Active under cost allocation tags.
tips: Pricing Calculator estimates before you build; Budgets alerts; Cost Explorer analyzes after the fact.

labs.title: Query data in S3 with Glue and Athena
labs.goal: Catalog a CSV file with a Glue crawler and analyze it with SQL in Athena.
labs.why: Serverless analytics with S3, Glue, and Athena is a Domain 3 topic (task 3.7).
labs.costNote: A short crawler run costs a few cents and the queries cost fractions of a cent.
steps:
Save this as sales.csv:
date,region,product,amount
2026-01-03,eu,shoes,120
2026-01-03,us,shoes,90
2026-01-04,eu,bags,200
2026-01-04,asia,bags,150
2026-01-05,us,hats,40
2026-01-05,asia,shoes,80
Create an S3 bucket lab-analytics-<number>. Upload sales.csv into a folder named sales/ and create an empty folder named athena-results/.
Open AWS Glue → Databases → Add database lab_db.
Open Glue → Crawlers → Create crawler lab-crawler with data source s3://lab-analytics-<number>/sales/, a new IAM role, and target database lab_db. Run it.
When the run finishes, open Tables in lab_db and look at the sales table and its columns.
Open Athena → Query editor → Settings and set the query result location to s3://lab-analytics-<number>/athena-results/.

Choose database lab_db and run:
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM sales
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY total DESC;
check: The crawler creates a table with date, region, product, and amount columns.
Athena returns totals for each region and shows how much data the query scanned.
cleanup: Delete the crawler lab-crawler, the table, and the database lab_db.
Delete the IAM role the crawler created.
Empty and delete the bucket lab-analytics-<number>.
tips: Athena is serverless: there was no cluster to create, and you paid only for the data scanned.

labs.title: Try the pre-trained AI services
labs.goal: Use the console demos of Rekognition, Comprehend, Translate, Polly, Textract, and Transcribe.
labs.why: Domain 3 expects you to match each AI service to the task it performs (task 3.7).
labs.costNote: A few demo requests cost cents at most. Don’t upload personal or sensitive images or documents.
steps: Open Rekognition → Label detection and upload a photo of an everyday scene. Try Text in image with a photo of a sign.
Open Comprehend → Real-time analysis and paste a short product review. Look at sentiment, entities, and key phrases.
Open Translate → Real-time translation and translate the same review into another language.
Open Polly → Text-to-speech, paste the translation, choose a voice for that language, and listen.
Open Textract → Try the demo with one of the sample documents and look at the extracted forms and tables.
Open Transcribe → Real-time transcription, allow microphone access, and speak a sentence.
check: Each service returns its result in seconds with no model training.
You can say in one line what each service is for.
tips: Images → Rekognition. Text insights → Comprehend. Documents → Textract. Speech to text → Transcribe. Text to speech → Polly.

labs.title: Deploy without managing servers: Elastic Beanstalk and Amplify
labs.goal: Deploy a sample app with Elastic Beanstalk and a static site with Amplify, and see what each manages for you.
labs.why: Comparing PaaS and managed hosting with EC2, and how responsibility shifts, is tested in Domains 2 and 3.
labs.costNote: The single-instance Beanstalk environment costs about $0.02 an hour. Amplify hosting for a tiny site costs cents at most.
steps: Open Elastic Beanstalk → Create application lab-eb. Choose a managed platform such as Python, the Sample application, and the Single instance (free tier eligible) preset.
If asked for an EC2 instance profile or service role, let the console create them (or follow its instructions to create them in IAM).
When the environment is healthy, open its URL. Then look at Configuration, Health, Events, and Logs.
In the EC2 console, find the instance and security group that Beanstalk created for you.
Create a folder containing an index.html file with a short message, and zip the folder’s contents.
Open AWS Amplify → Create new app → Deploy without Git, name it lab-amplify, and upload the zip. Open the generated URL.
check: Beanstalk created and manages the EC2 instance, security group, and monitoring from just a platform choice and code.
Amplify hosts the static site with HTTPS without any servers.
cleanup: Terminate the Beanstalk environment, then delete the application lab-eb.
Delete the Amplify app lab-amplify.
tips: You still own your code and data; AWS manages more of the platform as you move from EC2 to Beanstalk to Amplify.

labs.title: Governance and support tools
labs.goal: Review a workload with the Well-Architected Tool and explore AWS Health, support plans, and Organizations.
labs.why: The Well-Architected Framework, AWS Health, support plans, and Organizations are Domain 1, 2, and 4 topics.
steps: Open the Well-Architected Tool → Define workload named lab-webapp in your Region with the AWS Well-Architected Framework lens.
Answer a few questions in the Reliability and Cost Optimization pillars, then open the improvement plan.
Open AWS Health Dashboard → Your account health and look at open issues, scheduled changes, and the event log.
Open Support Center → Support plans and compare the plans (don’t change yours).
Open AWS Organizations (turned on in the first lab). Look at the root and create an organizational unit named Sandbox.
Open the Policies tab and read what service control policies (SCPs) do. Note that SCPs never restrict the management account.
check: The workload shows high and medium risks with links to improvement guidance.
You can name the difference between Business Support+, Enterprise, and Unified Operations.
cleanup: Delete the workload lab-webapp.
Delete the organizational unit Sandbox.
tips: Trusted Advisor checks the whole account automatically; the Well-Architected Tool reviews one workload through questions.
